name: Larnaca
title: UTM in Larnaca: Thickness Measurement at Anchor and Port
description: UTM and thickness measurement in Larnaca for ships in Larnaca Bay, the port and Vasilikos: pre-docking gauging, hull structure checks and scrubber piping.
h1: Ship Thickness Gauging in Larnaca Bay and at the Port of Larnaca
intro: Larnaca combines the island's main international airport with a broad bay where ships anchor for orders, crew changes and stores, a smaller commercial and passenger port, and the energy port at Vasilikos a short drive along the coast. For superintendents that makes it a practical place for short, well-prepared gauging jobs: the team can land, reach the launch and be aboard without a long transfer. We mobilise that team from India, with visas and port access arranged around the ship's expected time at anchor.

highlights.h: Airport on the shore of the bay
highlights.p: Larnaca International Airport sits on the coast beside the bay, which shortens the gap between the team's arrival and boarding and makes tight anchorage windows workable when the scope is agreed beforehand.
Most Larnaca work is on ships at anchor in the bay. Launches are booked through the agent, and the plan allows for the bay's exposure to easterly weather, which can interrupt boat transfers.
Tankers calling at the Vasilikos energy terminal on the south coast can be gauged on deck, deck piping and ballast spaces within terminal rules, often in the same trip as a Larnaca anchorage job.

port.h: Larnaca: bay anchorage, port and the Vasilikos energy terminal
p: Larnaca lies on the south-east coast of Cyprus, at the head of a wide bay between Cape Kiti and Cape Pyla. The port of Larnaca is small beside Limassol and handles a mix of general cargo, passenger and cruise calls, and the area's maritime activity is spread along the coast rather than concentrated in one harbour. The bay itself is the main asset: open water close to the airport, where ships stop for crew changes, provisions, spares, bunkers or orders while trading through the eastern Mediterranean.

The ships seen here are a cross-section of eastern Mediterranean traffic: product and chemical tankers, bulk carriers, general cargo and multipurpose ships, container feeders and offshore vessels, with tankers also calling at Vasilikos to the south-west. Many work regional routes linking Cyprus, the Levant, Egypt and the Aegean. Others stop at Larnaca simply because it is a convenient place to swap crew and take on supplies between Suez and Europe. Stays are typically short, from hours to a few days, so ships rarely stop here for the purpose of inspection, but a stop already planned for other reasons can carry targeted gauging if the preparation is done before arrival.

That defines inspection demand in Larnaca. The jobs are focused: a set of ballast tanks the superintendent is worried about, hatch covers before a grain charter, deck and piping readings on a tanker before vetting, or a pre-purchase snapshot of a ship whose buyer's representative flies in for the day. Managers who run their fleets from Limassol or Nicosia can also use Larnaca calls to check ships between dockings, because the airport makes attendance simple. When gauging reveals more than expected, the readings become the basis for a pre-docking scope to send to yards abroad, since heavy steel renewal on ocean-going ships is normally done in Greek, Turkish or other yards.

facilities.h: Where we take readings around Larnaca
p: Anchorage work dominates. The agent books a launch from the port, the team boards with portable gauges and couplant, and the crew will have opened, ventilated and certified the agreed spaces before arrival so that gauging starts without delay. Where tanks cannot be made safe in time, we work on deck, hatch covers, coamings and accessible piping first, and return to the tanks if the stay allows. The bay's exposure means a strong easterly or south-easterly can stop launches, so we schedule with a margin and keep the master informed of any change.

Work alongside is less common but straightforward: general cargo and passenger ships in the port of Larnaca, and tankers at Vasilikos, where the terminal's permit rules set what may be done during cargo operations. Because distances on the island are short, a single mobilisation can cover a ship at Larnaca, a call at Vasilikos and a job at the port of Limassol on consecutive days, which is often the most sensible way to use a visa period for a Cyprus programme. For ship inspection at a Cyprus anchorage, the limiting factor is almost never distance; it is whether the spaces are ready.
list: Larnaca Bay anchorage — targeted gauging on ships stopping for crew changes, stores, bunkers or orders, boarded by launch from the port
Port of Larnaca — gauging on general cargo, passenger and cruise vessels during port stays, arranged through the agent under ISPS rules
Vasilikos port — deck, deck piping and ballast tank gauging on tankers at the energy terminal within its permit-to-work system
Limassol port and anchorage — combined programmes with Larnaca calls, reached by road within the same mobilisation

context.h: Port state control, emissions rules and eastern Mediterranean trade
p: Cyprus takes part in both the Paris MoU and the Mediterranean MoU on port state control, and applies EU maritime law, so EU ETS (from 2024) and FuelEU Maritime (from 2025) cover voyages calling at Larnaca and Vasilikos. The Mediterranean SOx emission control area, in force since 1 May 2025, applies in Cypriot waters. For older tankers and bulk carriers that kept running on high-sulphur fuel with open-loop scrubbers, the overboard discharge sections and wash-water lines are the parts that tend to thin first, and a call off Larnaca is a reasonable moment to check them before a leak forces the issue.

Commercially, Larnaca sits close to the Levant and Egyptian ports and to the approaches to the Suez Canal, which brings a steady flow of ships past the island. Owners of ships on these regional trades, often older bulk carriers, general cargo ships and small tankers, face frequent charterer and vetting inspections and periodic sale and purchase activity. Each of those creates a reason to gauge, and a Larnaca stop is a convenient setting because the ship is quiet at anchor and the attending superintendent can fly in and out in a day.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Larnaca
jobs.p: The typical Larnaca job is short, focused and planned from a distance. The superintendent defines a handful of spaces and a question; the crew prepares the spaces before the ship arrives; we board as soon as the launch is free and work through the agreed list, passing readings back while the ship is still at anchor so a decision can be taken before it sails.
list: Ballast tank gauging on an older Handysize bulk carrier at anchor during a crew change, checking whether known wastage on side shell longitudinals had advanced since the last survey.
Hatch cover and coaming gauging on a general cargo ship before a grain fixture, carried out during a stores call in Larnaca Bay.
Deck plating and deck piping readings on a product tanker at Vasilikos, prepared for an upcoming oil-major vetting inspection and checked against the last thickness report.
Pre-purchase snapshot gauging on a multipurpose ship at anchor, with the buyer's superintendent flying in to attend and review readings on board.
Scrubber overboard piping inspection on a bulk carrier at anchor after the crew reported weeping at a discharge flange near the shell connection.

logistics: The team flies into Larnaca International Airport, which lies on the shore of the bay close to the port, with Paphos as an alternative. Launch boats for the anchorage, port passes under ISPS and terminal access at Vasilikos are arranged through the ship's agent, with our crew list, certificates and equipment details sent ahead. Each technician needs a visa for Cyprus, and we check the current entry requirements for every name on the crew list at enquiry. Because anchorage calls are often fixed at short notice, telling us about likely Larnaca stops early lets us hold visas ready for the window.

faqs.q: How much can be gauged during a short stop off Larnaca?
faqs.a: It depends far more on preparation than on time. If the crew has opened, ventilated and certified the agreed tanks before arrival, a day at anchor can cover several ballast tanks plus deck and hatch cover readings. If spaces are not ready, the time goes on waiting. We send a preparation checklist with the scope so the master can plan ahead.

faqs.q: Can you board at Larnaca anchorage at night or in poor weather?
faqs.a: Boarding times and conditions are set by the launch operator, the agent and the master, not by us, and we follow their decisions. Night transfers and transfers in a building easterly sea are often not allowed. We plan anchorage jobs with spare time for that reason and tell you early if weather is likely to cut the window.

faqs.q: Can one mobilisation cover Larnaca, Vasilikos and Limassol?
faqs.a: Yes. The three are close together by road, and combining calls is one of the practical advantages of working in Cyprus. Give us the ships and their expected windows and we will plan the order of jobs, the visa period and the agent arrangements as one trip.

faqs.q: Do you provide gauging for a pre-purchase inspection at anchor?
faqs.a: Yes, as a condition snapshot. In a short call we focus on the areas that tell a buyer most: hatch covers, coamings and hold plating on bulk carriers, ballast tanks and deck on tankers, and any areas the class records show as substantially corroded. It does not replace a renewal survey, but it gives the buyer measured facts to set beside the records.
